title: Why Households Are Deleveraging
text:
Why Households Are Deleveraging

Wei He, Xiaoxi Zhang

Gavekal Dragonomics | 18 Sep 2026

Bank lending to Chinese households is in outright decline in 2026 for the first time in history: a 1.6% YoY drop as of August, a striking change from the breakneck pace of expansion only a few years ago. This deleveraging could be interpreted as a sign of household caution—and after years of labor-market weakness, slowing income growth and declining property values, households have indeed become more risk-averse. But the decline in debt is also driven by a top-level decision made several years ago to tighten regulation in the finance and property sectors.The government’s efforts to restrict lending to real-estate developers triggered the property crash in 2021, with ramifications for housing sales and mortgage lending that are still playing out today. Less well-known is that financial regulators have also been steadily pushing for banks and consumer finance companies to reduce lending to high-risk household borrowers. The government is now attempting to soften the impact of that tightening by subsidizing consumer loans. Yet the fundamental regulatory stance still prioritizes risk control over growth, which means household deleveraging is likely to continue.
